Mark
mark
n. and v. (a target aimed at; a sign set upon a person or thing; rendering Hebrew tav and mattara, Greek skopos and stigma)
From the Saxon mearc, a boundary, sign, or limit — the same root as march, a border territory. The two English senses, a target and a brand, both descend from the idea of something set to be noticed.

Biblical Definition

Mark runs along two lines in the Authorized Version. The first is a target. “I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:14) — Greek skopos, the thing a runner fixes his eye on, the same root that gives us scope. Jonathan uses it in the plain sense, shooting arrows “as though I shot at a mark” (1 Samuel 20:20). Paul's image is exact: a runner who looks anywhere but at the mark loses the line, and the Christian life has one fixed point of attention. The second line is a sign set upon a person, and it cuts both ways. In Ezekiel the man with the writer's inkhorn is sent to “set a mark upon the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry for all the abominations that be done in the midst thereof” (Ezekiel 9:4) — the marked are those grieved by the sin of their own city, and the mark preserves them when judgment falls. Paul bears a different kind: “I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus” (Galatians 6:17), Greek stigmata, the brand burned on a slave to show whose he was. Scarred by stoning and scourging, Paul claims those wounds as ownership papers. The two lines meet in the sufferer, who finds himself the target: “He hath bent his bow, and set me as a mark for the arrow” (Lamentations 3:12) — and it is worth noting where that verse sits, some twenty lines before his compassions fail not; they are new every morning. Against all these stands the counterfeit mark of Revelation, by which a later power brands its own.

Webster 1828 Definition

A target, and a sign set upon a person. Paul presses toward the mark and bears the slave-brand of Christ; Ezekiel's mark preserves those who grieve over their city's sin.

expand to see more

MARK, n. [Sax. mearc, a bound, limit, sign.] A visible line, character or impression, made on any thing.

2. A character made by a person who cannot write his name, and intended as a substitute for it.

3. Any thing set up to be aimed at; hence, the object of aim, or that to which the mind is directed.

4. A distinguishing badge or sign; as the marks of a good man.

5. MARK, v.t. To observe; to note; to take notice of; as, mark my words.

Key Scripture

Philippians 3:14 — "I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus."

Ezekiel 9:4 — "And the LORD said unto him, Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and set a mark upon the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry for all the abominations that be done in the midst thereof."

Lamentations 3:12 — "He hath bent his bow, and set me as a mark for the arrow."

1 Samuel 20:20 — "And I will shoot three arrows on the side thereof, as though I shot at a mark."

Modern Corruption

The mark of Ezekiel 9 — set on those who grieve over the sin of their own people — is little known, while endless speculation attaches to the mark of Revelation and identifies it with each generation's new technology.

expand to see more

A vast popular literature, most of it dispensational in framework, has fixed the church's attention on identifying the mark of the beast with whatever means of commerce is newest — a barcode, a chip, a payment system — and each identification has aged badly. The framework itself is a nineteenth-century novelty, unknown to any Reformation confession, and the confidence with which it dates and diagrams the last things exceeds what Scripture gives. Meanwhile Ezekiel 9:4, which is about a mark actually set on real people by God, goes largely unpreached. There the marked are not those who escaped the culture but those who sigh and cry over the abominations done in the midst of their own city — men who did not merely disapprove of their nation's sin but grieved over it.

The principle to recover is Paul's single point of attention. I press toward the mark (Philippians 3:14) is written by a man who has just listed everything he might have looked at instead — his pedigree, his tribe, his blameless record in the law — and counted it loss. A runner cannot watch two things. The marks he does accept are the ones burned into his body by opposition, and he names them as a slave names his master's brand: they settle whose he is, and they end the argument.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tav is a mark or signature, the last letter of the alphabet, set on the foreheads in Ezekiel 9. Greek skopos is a goal watched; stigma, a brand burned on a slave.

expand to see more

Hebrew tav (H8420) — a mark, a signature; the sign set on the mourners' foreheads, Ezekiel 9:4.

Hebrew mattara (H4307) — a target, a mark to shoot at; Jonathan's arrows in 1 Samuel 20.

Greek skopos (G4649) — a goal fixed on by the eye; the mark of Philippians 3:14.

Greek stigma (G4742) — a brand pricked or burned on a slave; the marks of the Lord Jesus.

Greek charagma (G5480) — a stamp or graven mark; the word used of the mark of the beast.

Usage

"Of the runner's single object: I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling (Philippians 3:14)."

"Of a mark of preservation on mourners: set a mark upon the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry (Ezekiel 9:4)."

"Of the slave-brand of ownership: I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus (Galatians 6:17)."
